# In Praise of Wandering

There is a particular pleasure in walking down a street you have never seen before. Not with the purpose of reaching a monument or a well-reviewed café, but simply walking, letting the world unfold at its own pace. I remember doing this as a child: leaving the house with no firm plan, following the sidewalk until it turned to gravel, then to a dirt path, then to a field. The world seemed enormous because I was willing to get lost. Somewhere along that path I learned something that formal education later tried to teach out of me: that the most valuable discoveries are made when you are not looking for anything in particular.

Wandering is perhaps the oldest human way of thinking. Before we had maps, we had stories; before we had destinations, we had curiosity. To wander is to allow the world to ask a question of you, rather than forcing the world to answer yours. Our age, however, is not kind to wandering. We optimize our commutes, schedule our weekends, measure our steps and our screen time. Every app asks what we are looking for. The idea of moving through space—or through thought—without a goal can feel almost immoral, like wasting time. But time spent wandering is never wasted. It is the soil out of which meaning grows.

Consider walking. Not the purposeful power-walk of someone trying to get in their ten thousand steps, but the slow, open-ended stroll of someone who has nowhere to be. There is a reason the French have the word *flâneur*, a man who saunters around observing society, and it is not because they wanted an excuse to be lazy. The flâneur is a kind of philosopher, reading the city as if it were a book. In every shop window, every face, every half-heard conversation, there is a story. The wanderer notices a small crack in a wall where a vine has taken root. He sees an old woman feeding pigeons in a square that no one else seems to use. He hears a busker playing a song he has never heard, and for a moment the whole street stops to listen. None of this appears in any itinerary. None of it can be Googled. It can only be encountered.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who did some of his best thinking while walking in the countryside, wrote: “I can only meditate when I am walking. When I stop, I cease to think; my mind only works with my legs.” Many great thinkers have felt the same. The philosopher Søren Kierkegaard took long walks through Copenhagen, dashing back to his desk to write what had come to him. Henry David Thoreau walked several hours a day, insisting that “the moment my legs begin to move, my thoughts begin to flow.” This is not a coincidence. There is a rhythm to walking—the swing of the arms, the steady pulse of the feet—that seems to unlock something in the mind. It is as if the body, while moving through space, gives the mind permission to move through time: backward into memory, forward into possibility, sideways into association.

Neuroscientists have begun to explain what the poets always knew. When we are not focused on a task, the brain enters something called the default mode network. This is the network that lights up when we daydream, when we stare out a window, when our attention drifts. It is the network associated with creativity, with making connections between distant ideas, with imagining alternative futures. In other words, the brain is never really idle. When we think we are doing nothing, we are actually doing something profound. We are wandering through our own mental landscapes, and that wandering is what allows us to solve problems that resistance to focused thought cannot crack.

How many of us have had a brilliant idea in the shower? How many have found the answer to a stubborn problem while out for a run? The insight appears as if from nowhere, but it was not nowhere. It was the result of a long process of incubation, one that required periods of relaxation and openness. The creative mind works by alternating between focus and diffuse attention. A problem is attacked directly for a while, then abandoned. The unconscious keeps chewing on it. And then, at the most unexpected moment, the solution appears. Archimedes did not discover his principle while He was seated at a desk. He was in a bath, relaxing, and the water spilled over the edge. Newton did not formulate the law of gravity while laboriously calculating orbits. He was sitting under a tree, watching an apple fall. Whether or not these stories are literally true, they capture an important truth: the greatest breakthroughs often arrive at the edges of consciousness, in the margins of purposeful effort.

Wandering, then, is not the opposite of thinking. It is a different kind of thinking, one that honors the mysterious way the mind actually works. It is a mode of attention that is less controlled but more alert. The poet William Wordsworth wrote that poetry “takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.” But tranquillity, for Wordsworth, was not passivity. It was a kind of walking meditation. He composed many of his most famous poems while striding through the Lake District, muttering to himself, pausing to look at a flower or a cloud. The landscape was not just a backdrop for his poetry; it was a participant in it. The hills, the waters, the sheep, the ruined abbeys—these were the elements out of which he built his inner world.

There is a reason that so many spiritual traditions use the image of the path. The pilgrim has no illusions that the road is comfortable. The road is where the soul is tested and transformed. In Dante’s *Divine Comedy*, the poem begins with a man who, halfway through his life, finds himself lost in a dark wood. The whole of his journey—through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise—is a wandering guided by love and grace. He does not know where each step will lead. He must trust the road. Similarly, the ancient Greek hero Odysseus does not sail directly home from Troy. He wanders for ten years, encountering cyclopes, sirens, witches, and the land of the dead. His journey is a circle, but within that circle is the entire ocean of human experience. The *Odyssey* is the first great western novel precisely because it understands that the detour is the story. If Odysseus had gone straight home, there would be no epic. There would only be a weather report.

Narrative itself is a kind of wandering. A story begins with a disruption—a village burned, a letter delivered, a stranger walking into town—and then it follows the protagonist as she wanders in search of a solution. The middle of a story is full of unpredictable roads, false leads, and sudden discoveries. The reader, like the protagonist, does not know what will happen next. That uncertainty is the engine of meaning. We do not read stories to know the ending. We read them to dwell in the middle, to wander through the details of another life. A good book is not a bullet train to a conclusion. It is a labyrinth, and the pleasure is in getting lost.

Wandering also shapes the way we know places. There is a huge difference between visiting a city as a tourist, following a map from one famous landmark to another, and walking into a neighborhood where no one has told you to go. In the first case, the city is a sequence of pictures, already familiar from postcards. In the second, the city becomes three-dimensional, smells and sounds, textures and moods. You might turn a corner and find a bakery that has been there for eighty years. You might sit on a bench and watch a group of children playing soccer in the rain. You might get caught in an unexpected shower and duck into a doorway where you meet a retired violin maker who tells you his whole life story. None of this is efficient. But it is alive.

The twentieth-century movement known as psychogeography understood this deeply. The Situationists, led by Guy Debord, proposed a practice called the *dérive*—a drift through the urban landscape, guided by nothing but the feelings and encounters that arise along the way. Instead of treating the city as a set of routes to be navigated, the dérive treated it as a vast emotional terrain, full of currents and eddies. The goal was not to get somewhere. The goal was to let the city reveal itself, to become aware of the atmospheres and histories that official maps could not capture. For Debord, walking was a form of resistance. To drift was to refuse the logic of productivity, to reclaim the city as a space of play and wonder rather than commerce and traffic.

The idea of wandering as resistance resonates now more than ever. We live in a culture obsessed with optimization. Our language is full of words like *efficiency*, *deliverables*, *targets*, *scalability*. Social media encourages us to present our lives as a linear sequence of achievements. We are constantly told to be more productive, to read more books, to learn more skills, to monetize our hobbies. In such a culture, the simple act of wandering—of walking without a destination, of daydreaming, of following a whim—is almost subversive. It says: I am not a machine. I am not a resource to be optimized. I am a creature who is curious about the world. And curiosity, by definition, does not know what it is looking for. If it knew, it would no longer be curiosity.

Of course, not all wandering is leisurely. There is a kind of wandering that comes from displacement—the refugee who wanders because home is no longer safe, the exile who wanders because the borders of the world have closed around her. This is the dark side of wandering, the side we must never romanticize away. To wander unwillingly, without food or hope, is not freedom. It is suffering. We must be careful not to confuse the voluntary wandering of the flâneur with the forced wandering of the displaced. The first is a privilege; the second is a wound. But perhaps it is precisely this wound that has produced some of the most powerful art of our time. Exile, as many writers have noted, sharpens the memory. The person who has lost a homeland sees it more vividly than the person who has never left. The refugee's wandering is a kind of testimony, a remembering of what has been lost. And in that remembering, the wandering mind finds meaning.

Wandering through time is just as important as wandering through space. Memory is a strange, meandering path. We think we remember an event, but what we actually remember is the last time we remembered it. Each recollection is a new visit to an old place, and the place has changed. The French writer Marcel Proust built a two-thousand-page novel out of a single act of wandering memory. In *In Search of Lost Time*, the narrator tastes a madeleine dipped in tea, and suddenly the entire world of his childhood, with its church steeples and summer afternoons, floods into his mind. He does not follow a straight line. He follows scent, taste, emotion. The novel is a web of digressions, a endless wandering through time, and it is precisely this wandering that makes it feel true. Our own lives are not neatly chronological. They are made of moments, fragments, associations. When we let our minds wander, we are not wasting time. We are tracing the actual shape of our lives.

The same is true of the future. We often imagine that we should have a five-year plan, a clear map of where we are going. But nobody actually gets to a great life by following a blueprint. They arrive, as the novelist William Gibson put it, through a series of improvisations and accidents. The career you end up loving is the one you discovered by chance. The friendship that sustains you begins with a random conversation. The book that changes you is the one you picked up because you liked the cover. This is not a plea for chaos. It is a plea for openness. The future, like a landscape, is too vast to be mapped in advance. The best we can do is have a compass, a vague sense of direction, and the courage to wander.

In the Middle Ages, before the printing press, scholars used a word for the act of reading: *legere*. It meant to gather, to select, to wander among the texts. A reader was not a passive consumer. She was a wanderer, moving from one insight to another, making her own path through the forest of words. When we read today, we often want everything immediately: summaries, key takeaways, five bullet points. But the richness of reading lies in the detours, in the passages that have nothing to do with the thesis, in the long descriptions of weather and landscape and clothing that seem irrelevant until they become unforgettable. Literature is an invitation to wander. To read closely is to walk slowly.

There is also a sacred dimension to wandering. The pilgrimage, as old as humanity, is a journey to a holy place. But the real holiness lies not in the destination but in the walking itself. The medieval pilgrims who walked from Chartres to Santiago de Compostela did not simply want to arrive. They wanted to be changed by the road. They sought hunger, fatigue, the open sky, the encounter with strangers. They carried few things, because the journey required them to let go. The tradition of the *wanderer* runs through every religion: the Buddha leaving his palace to walk the dusty roads of India, Jesus wandering through Galilee with nowhere to lay his head, the Sufi dervishes who traveled as a form of prayer. Wandering is not a retreat from the world. It is a way of being in the world, a way of paying attention to the mystery that surrounds us. Every step is a prayer. Every road is a revelation.

What does it mean to dwell? Martin Heidegger wrote that the essence of human life is “dwelling.” But dwelling, for him, did not mean owning a house. It meant belonging—being rooted, being attuned to the place where you live. How do we come to dwell in a place? Not by buying property, but by knowing the place intimately. And the only way to know a place intimately is to wander through it, again and again, letting it become part of your body. The wanderer knows where the sun rises on the plaza, where the first leaves fall in autumn, which café has the strong coffee and which has the good conversation. To dwell is to have a relationship with a place, and relationships require time. They require wandering hand in hand through the ordinary days. The city that you have wandered through is a city you will never forget. It has become a part of your internal landscape.

I have noticed that my own best thoughts do not come at the desk. They come while I am washing the dishes, folding laundry, walking to the store, staring at the sky. They come when I'm not trying to think. The moment I try to seize them, they vanish. The mind is like a small animal that approaches only when you are still and quiet. If you chase it, it runs. But if you sit, or walk, and let your thoughts drift, it comes and sits beside you. This is the wisdom of the wanderer: nothing of importance can be forced. Our greatest insights are given to us, not produced. We can prepare the ground, and then we must wait. The waiting is not passivity. It is a kind of active openness, a wandering through the fields of the possible.

The universal experience of taking a shower and suddenly solving the problem you have been wrestling with for days is a perfect image of this. The water is warm, the mind is unoccupied, and for a few moments you are not trying to be anywhere. You are somewhere within yourself. The answer appears, not because you demanded it, but because you let it. There is a Spanish proverb that says: *Hitch your wagon to a star, but take the longest road*—perhaps because the longest road is the one that offers the most chances for transformation. If we always take the straightest line, we will miss everything that lies between our origin and our destination. And what lies between is most of life.

We need to reclaim the right to wander. We need to be unembarrassed about taking a walk for no reason, about staring out the window, about letting a Sunday afternoon dissolve into nothing. We need to remember that the best conversations are the ones that ramble, that one topic leads to another, and we end up somewhere we never expected. We need to allow our children to get bored, because boredom is the beginning of creativity. A child who is bored must invent, must wander, must find something that does not exist yet. The child who is scheduled from morning to night never learns to listen to the inner voice. The inner voice speaks quietly, and it speaks in a way that is not linear. It takes detours. It follows fragments. It changes its mind. It needs room.

In the end, wandering is not about going nowhere. It is about going somewhere without knowing where that is. It is an act of trust in the unknown. The world is vast and full of beauty, but we will not see it from the highway. We will see it from the side roads, the footpaths, the alleys that no guidebook mentions. We will see it when we are willing to get lost. Getting lost is how we find things—not the things we thought we were looking for, but the things that we did not know we needed. It is how we find ourselves.

So wander. Wander with your feet and with your mind. Wander in the garden, in the library, in the long memory of the night. Wander through the neighborhoods of your own heart. Do not ask where you will end up. Ask what you will notice along the way. The universe is not a checkpoint; it is a cloud, shimmering with possibility. Every step is a sentence in a story you cannot yet read. Every corner is a door. Every road asks the same question, the oldest question in the world: *What do you see?* And the only answer worth giving, from a wanderer, is: *I don't know yet. Let me look.*
